title: Dinner for People Who Disagree
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
Katara came home carrying a bag of dried fish and three new reasons to argue with the council.

I met her at the Riverstone Door.

For one second I forgot everything except the fact that she was standing there. Her hair was windblown, her cheeks red from the journey, and the strap of her travel bag had left a mark across her shoulder.

"You're home," I said.

"I am."

I hugged her before I remembered to ask.

She laughed against my neck and held me tight.

"Missed you," she whispered.

"Missed you too."

When we stepped apart, she looked over my shoulder.

"Where are the others?"

"Aang is trying to convince Toph that a dinner menu can be planned without threats."

"That sounds promising."

"It is not."

Katara grinned.

The Southern clinic had enough trained staff to manage the next phase without her. She'd helped set up a treatment room, trained two local healers in the new record system, and arranged for supplies that were actually available rather than inventing a list of things nobody could deliver. The work would continue without her; that mattered.

At the house, Toph heard us before we reached the steps.

"Well, look who remembered the way home."

Katara set down her bag.

"Missed you too."

Toph crossed the room in three quick strides and hugged her, muttering something about sea air and terrible timing.

Aang came from the kitchen with flour on his sleeve.

He stopped.

For once, he had no words at all.

Katara looked at him.

"Hello, Aang."

He crossed the room and hugged her so carefully that she laughed.

"I'm not made of glass."

"I know."

"You're holding me like a teacup."

"Then let me put you down before I spill."

We all laughed.

I wished the evening could have stayed there.

Instead, Iroh arrived for dinner, and the first argument began over the place settings.

Toph wanted to sit nearest the open window because it gave her the best sense of the street below. Katara wanted the window closed because the evening was cold. Aang wanted the table moved so no one had to sit with their back to the door. I had planned six dishes and only counted five bowls.

Iroh examined the scene with a smile.

"May I offer a suggestion?"

"No," Toph said.

"Excellent. I shall keep it to myself."

That made her laugh.

We moved the table. We kept the window open a finger's width. Aang fetched another bowl. Iroh poured tea while Katara unpacked the dried fish she'd brought from home, which Toph promptly declared proof that Katara had missed us in a practical and delicious way.

Dinner began.

Then the council came up.

Katara had heard from the Southern healers that the floodplain repair plan still depended on one inspection committee. She worried that decisions were being delayed because nobody wanted to take responsibility for the cost. Aang thought the committee needed time to hear witnesses. Toph believed several members were using the delay as an excuse not to acknowledge their own mistakes.

"I don't want them to rush," Katara said. "I want them to make a decision."

Aang set down his cup.

"If they decide without hearing Sela, they'll repeat the problem."

"They have heard Sela."

"Not about the revised path."

Toph snorted.

"They've heard everyone. They just don't like the answer."

I looked at the table.

Iroh was eating quietly. He wasn't going to rescue us from the discomfort.

"Can we agree on what needs to happen next?" I asked.

"We need more evidence," Aang said.

"We need to use the evidence we have," Katara replied.

"We need a council that isn't afraid of dirt," Toph added.

"Toph."

"What? I can smell the fear."

I could feel myself becoming the person who wanted to make everyone happy before dessert. It was a familiar reflex. If I could turn the argument into a tidy plan, maybe no one would go to bed upset.

But the question wasn't actually simple.

"Let's separate the issues," I said. "Safety, timing, and accountability."

Aang had drawn a little bridge on the back of the supper menu. The bridge was smiling. He had given it eyebrows.

"Is that meant to persuade the council?" Toph asked.

"It's meant to remind us there's a bridge on the other side of all these arguments."

"Looks more like a caterpillar."

Katara set down her chopsticks. "There's a family whose vegetable plot is flooded every time that bridge backs up. They won't find your caterpillar reassuring."

Aang's ears went pink. "I know. I didn't mean—"

"I know what you meant." She rubbed a hand over her face. The journey home had left her tired, and we'd hardly given her time to take off her coat. "I just don't want to arrive tomorrow and find that we've spent another week discussing how to discuss it."

Toph leaned back. "Then go talk to the family. Ask Sela where the water actually comes up. Don't make me stamp a plan I haven't walked."

The room went quiet. Aang flattened the menu in front of him.

"I want a hearing because people deserve a say," he said, more slowly. "Not because I want to wait forever."

"And I want to protect them tonight," Katara answered, "not make their choices for them for the next ten years."

I stared at the dumplings cooling on the table. I knew all three of them loved one another in ways that weren't identical. I had told them separately that I was ethically non-monogamous and preferred polyamory. Somehow that made me especially tempted to turn every disagreement into proof we were doing relationships correctly.

But nobody had asked me to referee. I could love Katara's urgency, Aang's care and Toph's refusal to flatter an engineer without choosing one of them as tonight's winner.

"Can I make a suggestion that doesn't solve the bridge?" I asked.

Toph grinned. "Finally. A good suggestion."

"Let's eat before Katara has to catch another boat. Tomorrow we can write the questions we still need answered."

Katara looked at me as though she'd forgotten food existed. Then she took a bite of dumpling and closed her eyes.

"That's disgusting," she said fondly. "Who put so much pepper in these?"

"Toph," Aang and I said together.

"You're welcome," Toph replied.

We talked for another twenty minutes. We did not reach a perfect agreement.

Katara believed the current evidence justified temporary action to protect the gardens. Aang wanted the affected residents to sign off on the revised plan. Toph was willing to inspect temporary barriers but refused to let her assessment replace anyone else's testimony.

They were all making reasonable points.

I was frustrated anyway.

Iroh finally set down his cup.

"I wonder," he said, "whether tonight's dinner requires the council to have reached a decision."

Toph turned toward him.

"We're not going to solve the bridge by eating dumplings."

"No," he agreed. "But perhaps we can decide which part of the conversation belongs to tomorrow."

I looked at Katara.

She looked tired. Not just from travel, but from weeks of responsibility in a clinic where every decision had mattered. She'd come home, and we'd greeted her with another public problem.

"I'm sorry," I said.

She frowned.

"For what?"

"For acting like you had to arrive and fix everything immediately."

Her shoulders lowered.

"I don't mind talking about it. I mind that we keep turning every meal into a meeting."

Aang nodded.

"I do that."

"We all do," I said.

Toph took another dumpling.

"Speak for yourselves. I mostly turn meals into arguments about the food."

Katara laughed.

The tension eased without vanishing.

We almost made it to dessert before Katara remembered the shipment she had promised the Southern clinic.

"Did the bandages go?" she asked.

Aang and I looked at each other. He had been waiting for the revised list; I had assumed the delivery was already arranged. Toph made a noise suggesting she had been expecting precisely this mistake.

Katara reached for her travel bag. I caught myself preparing to apologize and volunteer her for another hour of work.

"Can we see the list first?" I asked.

It asked for two boxes of clean bandages, copies of the training notes, and a replacement stove valve. The local healers were already making their own treatment decisions. Nobody needed Katara to go back tomorrow and rescue them from an ordinary delivery.

"I can ask whether the Threadway keeper has a safe parcel window," Aang said.

"Ask," Toph repeated. "Don't dump a job on them."

"Ask," Aang agreed.

Toph offered to check the valve measurements if someone brought them to her workshop. I wrote down the person responsible for each task so Katara didn't have to remember everything after a long journey.

Iroh regarded our makeshift list. "You've turned dessert into a council meeting."

"We're remarkably gifted at it," I admitted.

"Then adjourn."

We did. Toph asked Katara what she'd enjoyed most while away, and Katara answered with a story about two young healers arguing over the best way to label a drawer. Aang confessed that his last kite had spun in circles. Toph requested a demonstration so she could make fun of it accurately.

Later I asked what each of us wanted tomorrow. Aang wanted a walk, Toph an uninterrupted hour, Katara breakfast in her own home. We agreed on breakfast and left the rest open. Polyamory didn't mean flattening three people into one set of wants. It meant listening to the differences without making anybody compete for a place at the table.


After dinner, Iroh helped dry the dishes. He didn't comment on our relationship structure, though he knew Jasper's commitments were openly non-monogamous and consensual. He had never treated our household as an interesting problem to solve. He simply washed the cups and asked where we kept the towels.

When he left, Katara walked with me to the garden.

The night smelled of wet stone and the first flowers of the sea-glass orchard carried on the wind. I took her hand.

"Are you really back for a while?" I asked.

"For now. The clinic can manage without me, and I need to remember that doesn't mean I failed them."

I squeezed her fingers.

"Good."

She looked at me.

"Did you miss me?"

"Every day."

"And did you have a life while I was gone?"

"Also every day."

She smiled.

"Good. I want you to."

I leaned closer.

"Can I kiss you?"

"Please."

Her kiss was warm and familiar, but not the same as before she'd left. There was new tiredness in her shoulders, new steadiness in her hands. We had both changed a little.

I liked that we could meet each other again.

Inside, Aang and Toph were arguing over the last dumpling. The argument ended when they split it.

Tomorrow we would return to the bridge. Tonight we closed the council notebook and made room at the table for the person who had come home.
